title: Problem Set 3
text:
Exercise 5: Opinion Dynamics
Download the Facebook100 data, containing facebook networks for 100 universities in the US. We want to analyze how the different networks generate different opinion dynamics. Keep the largest component of each network only.

rm(list=ls())
library(R.matlab)   # read .mat files
library(tidygraph)      # optimize data pipeline

# iterate thru files in facebook100
folder_path <- file.path("C:/Users/T14/7Programming/R/class/networks/problem_sets/ps03/data/facebook100")
file_list <- list.files(path = folder_path, 
                        pattern = "\\.mat$", 
                        full.names = TRUE)

facebook_graphs <- list() #init empty matrix

for (file in file_list){
  clean_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(file)) # extract school name
  raw_mat <- readMat(file)                                # load in sparse matrix object
  adj_matrix <- raw_mat$A                                 # extract adj matrix stored as "A"
  tbl_g <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(                   # convert to igraph object
    adj_matrix, 
    mode = "undirected",
    diag = FALSE # remove self-loops
  ) %>% 
    as_tbl_graph()                                        # store as a tidy graph object -- memory efficient
  facebook_graphs[[clean_name]] <- tbl_g                  # object store in list, end of iteration
}

rm(raw_mat, adj_matrix, tbl_g)                            # rm temporary objects -- free up memory
facebook_graphs$schools <- NULL                           # remove school names vector


(a) Assumption: ‘Listening’
To simplify things we will assume that each node “listens” to all her neighbors (and herself) with the same probability. In other words, we assume that \(T_{ij} = \frac{1}{(1 + d_i)}\) for all \(j \in N_i\) and also \(T_{ii} = \frac{1}{(1 + d_i)}\). The assumption that the node listens to herself with the same weight makes the walk “lazy,” which guarantees aperiodicity (which will be needed for convergence to consensus later on).


(b) Assign Probabilities
We will simulate innate/original opinions from a uniform(0,1); i.e., we will assign to each node a \(p_i(0)\) that is drawn from a uniform random variable. This means that the consensus should land near 0.5 for every network by the LLN (since these networks have thousands of nodes), and any deviation from that is informative about how concentrated the influence is in the network. If a few high-degree nodes happen to have extreme opinions, and those nodes dominate the stationary distribution, we should see the consensus pulled away from the expected value of 0.5.


(c) Maximum & Median Influence
We know from the Convergence to Consensus proposition (Golub & Jackson) that, if T is irreducible, the following are equivalent:

T is convergent
T is aperiodic
T has a unique (positive) left-eigenvector \(s\) corresponding to eigenvalue 1 with \(\sum s_i = 1\) such that for every \(p \in [0, 1]^n\):

\[
\left(lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} T^t p \right)_i = sp  
\]
for every individual \(i \in N\).
Furthermore, we know that consensus is defined as: limiting beliefs are all equal to a weighted average of initial beliefs, with agent \(i\)’s weight (or influence) given by \(s_i\).
The influence vector \(s_i\) given by the left eigenvector of \(T\):

Note that \(\lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} T^t p = \lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} T^t (Tp)\)
It must be that \(sp = sTp\) for every \(p \in [0,1]^n\)
This implies that \(s = sT\)

The eigenvector property says that, for all \(i\):
\[
s_i = \sum_{j \in N} T_{ji}s_j
\]

The influence of \(i\) is the weighted sum of the influences of individuals \(j\) that pay attention to \(i\)

Influence of \(j\) is weighted by \(T_{ji}\) which is the trust \(j\) places on \(i\)


Thus, to impute the influence of a network we must compute the left eigenvector of \(T\). So do so, we must find the vector \(s\) such that \(sT = s \iff T's = s\).

test <- facebook_graphs$American75

To find the left-eigenvalue, we must build a function that converges to \(s\) after iterating through multiplications of \(T'\). We start by giving everyone equal influence, after which we multiply this starting vector by a weighted combination of the values of nodes that listen to it. We then normalize to ensure the values sum to 1. We iterate through this process until we reach some threshold, such that any change in our multiplication step does not significantly update the influence vector values. First, we must build a ‘listening’ matrix to get an idea of how much each node listens to others.

library(Matrix) # fast method: using as_edgelist

listening_matrix <- function(graph_obj){ # input: graph (network) object
  n = vcount(graph_obj)
  degree = degree(graph_obj)
  weight = 1 / (1 + degree) # via assumption from part (a)
  
  edgelist <- as_edgelist(graph_obj)                             # two-column matrix of edges
  rows <- c(1:n, edgelist[,1], edgelist[,2])                     # diagonal + both directions
  cols <- c(1:n, edgelist[,2], edgelist[,1])                   
  vals <- c(weight, weight[edgelist[,1]], weight[edgelist[,2]])  # self-loops; i listen to j; j listen to i
  
  sparseMatrix(i = rows, # return of a sparse matrix of final listening matx
               j = cols, 
               x = vals, 
               dims = c(n, n))
}


# sanity check
test_listening_mat <- listening_matrix(test)
test_listening_mat[1:10, 1:10] # looks good

Now that our listening matrix function works well, we will build the left-eigenvalue function, which takes this listening matrix as an input, as well as optional arguments regarding the tolerance (how much the influence vector changes for the function to return) as well as the max number of iterations through the function (set as 10_000)

left_eigenvector <- function(listening_mx,                 # inputs: - listening matrix       
                            tol = 0.00001,                #         - threshold to determine convergence
                            max_it = 10000){              #         - max num iterations thru loop
  n <- nrow(listening_mx)   # num of rows in tmat (corresponds to )
  s <- rep(1/n, n)          # set starting influence vector as equal across all nodes
  T_trans <- t(listening_mx) # transpose listening mat to perform T's
  for (i in seq_len(max_it)) { # iterative process: keep updating s until we 'converge'
    s_new <- T_trans %*% s               # matrix multpl
    s_new <- s_new / sum(s_new)          # normalize
    if (max(abs(s_new - s)) < tol) break # stop condition only if we hit below arbitrary threshold value
    s <- s_new                           # update s vector as newly multiplied vect
  }
  return(as.vector(s_new))
}


# sanity check
test_lft_eigen <- left_eigenvector(listening_mx = test_listening_mat)
length(test_lft_eigen) == vcount(test) # should match num nodes from original network: yes

[1] TRUE



# loop over all networks, collect all influence scores
all_influences <- c()
for (name in names(facebook_graphs)) {
  g <- facebook_graphs[[name]]    # extract graph object from specified matrix
  T_mat <- listening_matrix(g)    # get associated lsitening mat
  s <- left_eigenvector(T_mat)    # get associated left-eigenvector
  all_influences <- c(all_influences, s) # append to list
}


# histogram
hist(all_influences, breaks = 500, col = "goldenrod",
     main = "Influence Distribution Across Facebook100 Networks",
     xlab = "Influence score", ylab = "Frequency", xlim = c(0, 0.0012))







# summary stats
cat("max influence:   ", max(all_influences), "\n")

max influence:    0.008119159 

cat("median influence:", median(all_influences), "\n")

median influence: 4.401269e-05 


After plotting, we notice that the influence is highly skewed across nodes, with our histogram displaying a strong right-skew, with majority of the observations lying near very low influence (left of the median of 0.000044) and a max value ranging to 0.008. This suggests a power-law like structure, which we can check by plotting the complementary CDF:

df <- data.frame(influence = sort(all_influences, 
                                  decreasing = TRUE)) # arrange influence in desc order
df$rank <- 1:nrow(df)                                 # rank given as row number
df$ccdf <- df$rank / nrow(df)                         # calc complementary cdf val as: (rank)/(total # of obs)

ggplot(df, aes(x = influence, y = ccdf)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.3, color = "salmon") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +   # log-log scale
  labs(x = "Influence (log)", y = "PDF (log)") +
  theme_bw()








The plot suggests that perhaps the distribution follows a log-normal structure, or some other family of exponential functions.


(d) Histogram of Consensus Opinions
To plot a histogram of the consensus opinions, we need to generate the consensus opinions given by the relationship \(\sum_{j \in P} s_jp_j(0)\)

# consensus vector
consensus <- c()
for (name in names(facebook_graphs)) {
  g     <- facebook_graphs[[name]]       # extract graph network
  T_mat <- listening_matrix(g)           # generate listening matrix
  s     <- left_eigenvector(T_mat)       # find left eigenvector
  p0    <- runif(vcount(g))              # random initial opinions (random uniform based on n nodes)
  consensus <- c(consensus, sum(s * p0)) # s · p0: store in consensus vector
}

# sanity check
length(consensus) # 100; checks out

[1] 100



# histogram
ggplot(data.frame(consensus = consensus), aes(x = consensus)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "forestgreen", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Consensus opinion p(inf)", y = "Number of networks",
       title = "Consensus Opinions Across Facebook100 Networks") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust=0.5))







# modal bin
h <- hist(consensus, breaks = 25, plot = FALSE) # calculate hist values without plotting
modal_mid <- h$mids[which.max(h$counts)]        # extra max counts from each bin
cat("modal consensus opinion:", round(modal_mid, 3), "\n")

modal consensus opinion: 0.5 

cat("mean consensus opinion: ", round(mean(consensus), 4), "\n")

mean consensus opinion:  0.4998 


The histogram shows that consensus opinions are tightly concentrated around 0.5 across all 100 networks, with a modal value of 0.501 and a mean of 0.5006. This is to be expected, as initial opinions are drawn iid from unif(0,1) dist with mean 0.5, and the influence weights sum to 1, the consensus \(\sum_j s_j p_j(0)\) is a weighted average of many independent draws, which concentrates around 0.5 by LLN.


(e) Speed of Learning Calculation
Now we want to calculate the speed of learning. For each network, calculate the first period,
\(t^*\), where \(\left(\sum_i \tilde{d}_i(A)(p_i(t) - p_i(\infty))^2 \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} < \varepsilon\) for \(\epsilon = 0.1\) and \(\tilde{d}_i(A) = \frac{d_i(A)}{\sum_i d_i(A)}\).
To do so, we simply calculate the time it takes to converge for a network:

convergence_time <- function(T_mat, p0, s, g, epsilon = 0.1) {
  consensus <- sum(s * p0)                # p_i(\infty)
  deg       <- degree(g)                  # d_i
  d_tilde   <- deg / sum(deg)             # \tilde{d}_i = d_i / \sum_i d_i
  p         <- p0                         # start at initial opinions
  
  for (t in 1:10000) {
    p     <- as.vector(T_mat %*% p)       # one round: everyone updates
    diff  <- p - consensus                # how far each node is from consensus
    error <- sqrt(sum(d_tilde * diff^2))  # weighted error
    if (error < epsilon) return(t)        # done? exit condition
  }
  return(NA)
}

After which, we apply to all 100 networks.

t_stars <- c() # init empty results list
for (name in names(facebook_graphs)) {
  g     <- facebook_graphs[[name]]
  T_mat <- listening_matrix(g)
  s     <- left_eigenvector(T_mat)
  p0    <- runif(vcount(g))
  t_star <- convergence_time(T_mat, p0, s, g) # t-star: how many iterations it takes to converge
  t_stars <- c(t_stars, t_star)               # append to our results list
}

# results
results <- data.frame(network = names(facebook_graphs), t_star = t_stars)
results <- results[order(results$t_star), ]
head(results)

     network t_star
1 American75      1
2  Amherst41      1
3   Auburn71      1
4   Baylor93      1
5       BC17      1
6 Berkeley13      1

cat("Fastest convergence:", min(t_stars), "\n")

Fastest convergence: 1 

cat("Slowest convergence:", max(t_stars), "\n")

Slowest convergence: 1 

cat("Median convergence: ", median(t_stars, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")

Median convergence:  1 


We see from the results that given an initial value \(\epsilon = 0.1\), all of our networks converge within one iteration, meaning that a single round of local averaging is sufficient to bring opinions within 0.1 of consensus across all 100 networks. This is because the networks are sufficiently large, so the degree-weighted averaging in one step already smooths out most of the disagreement from the random initial opinions.


(f) Second Eigenvalue Plot
We want to understand the relationship between network structure and the speed of learning. The second largest eigenvalue \(\lambda_2\) of the listening matrix \(T\) governs the rate at which opinions converge; specifically, disagreement decays at rate \(\lambda_2^t\), so networks with \(\lambda_2\) closer to 1 converge more slowly.
For each network, we compute the two largest eigenvalues of \(T\). The first eigenvalue is always 1, guaranteed by the row-stochastic property of \(T\) (each row sums to 1, making \(\mathbf{1}\) a right eigenvector with eigenvalue 1). The Perron-Frobenius theorem additionally guarantees that this is the dominant eigenvalue for irreducible non-negative matrices. We then take the modulus of the second eigenvalue \(\lambda_2\).

library(RSpectra) # library for computing eigenvalues of large sparse matrices

# compute the second largest eigenvalue (lambda2) for each network
lambda2s <- c()                                    # init empty vector to store lambda2 vals
for (name in names(facebook_graphs)) {             # loop over each uni
  g     <- facebook_graphs[[name]]                 # extract graph object
  T_mat <- listening_matrix(g)                     # build the listening matrix
  eigs  <- eigs(T_mat, k = 2, which = "LM")        # compute top 2 eigenvalues by largest magnitude
  lambda2s <- c(lambda2s, Mod(eigs$values[2]))     # modulus of 2nd eigenvalue (handles complex values)
}

We compute the convergence time \(t^*\) for each network at three progressively stricter thresholds: \(\varepsilon = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001\). For each network and threshold, we generate random initial opinions from a unif\((0,1)\) distribution, after which we run the opinion dynamics \(p(t) = Tp(t-1)\) iteratively, and record the first period \(t\) at which the degree-weighted error falls below \(\varepsilon\).

# compute t* for multiple epsilon thresholds to see how strictness affects convergence
epsilons <- c(0.1, 0.01, 0.001)                    # three thresholds for eps
all_results <- data.frame()                        # init df to store results

for (eps in epsilons) {                                        # loop over each epsilon value
  t_stars <- c()                                               # init empty vector for this epsilon's t* values
  for (name in names(facebook_graphs)) {                       # loop over each school
    g     <- facebook_graphs[[name]]                           # extract graph object
    T_mat <- listening_matrix(g)                               # build listening matrix
    s     <- left_eigenvector(T_mat)                           # compute influence vector
    p0    <- runif(vcount(g))                                  # generate random initial opinions
    t_star <- convergence_time(T_mat, p0, s, g, epsilon = eps) # compute convergence time
    t_stars <- c(t_stars, t_star)                              # append t* for this network
  }
  all_results <- rbind(all_results, data.frame(    # bind results for this epsilon to the full df
    lambda2 = lambda2s,                            # second eigenvalue
    t_star  = t_stars,                             # convergence time
    epsilon = paste0("epsilon = ", eps)                
  ))
}


# plot: lambda2 vs t* by each epsilon
ggplot(all_results, aes(x = lambda2, y = t_star)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~epsilon, scales = "free_y") + # separate panel per epsilon, y-axis scales independently
  labs(x = expression(lambda[2]),
       y = expression(t^"*"),
       title = expression(paste("Convergence Time vs ", lambda[2]))) +
  theme_bw()








At \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), all networks converge within a single iteration, meaning that the threshold is too lenient given the size and density of the Facebook100 networks. As we lower \(\varepsilon\), convergence times increase and a clear positive relationship with \(\lambda_2\) emerges. This suggests that networks whose second eigenvalue is closer to 1 take more rounds to reach consensus, confirming that \(\lambda_2\) governs the speed of learning. A value of \(\lambda_2\) near 1 indicates high modularity, meaning that loosely connected communities create a bottleneck that slows the diffusion of opinions across the network.

title: Random Effects
text:
As we saw with the pooled OLS estimator, it yields a consistent and unbiased estimator but is not efficient, due to the serial correlation in the composite error induced by the unobserved effect. Thus, there exists an estimator that is efficient under similar conditions, known as the Random Effects estimator; this is the equivalent to the generalized least squares (GLS) estimator from finite sample OLS.



Our assumptions here follow almost exactly the same from pooled OLS, with one slight change in assumption 5.


Same as before
\[
y_{it} = x_{it}'\beta + f_i + \mu_{it}
\]



Same as before
\[
\mathbb{E}[f_i \mid x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \cdots, x_{iT}] \equiv \mathbb{E}[f_i \mid X_i] = 0
\]



Same as before
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \cdots, x_{iT}, f_i] \equiv \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i] = 0
\]



Same as before
\[
\begin{cases}
  1. \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(f_i \mid X_i) = \sigma_{f}^2 &\text{Constant Variance in the Unobserved Error} \\
  2. \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i) = \sigma_{\mu}^2 & \text{Constant Variance in the Idiosyncratic Error} \\
  3. \mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\mu_{it}, \mu_{is}) = 0 \quad \forall_{t \neq s} & \text{No Serial Correlation}
\end{cases}
\]



SLIGHT MODIFICATION
\[
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i' V^{-1} X_i  \xrightarrow{p} \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(X_i'V^{-1}X_i)}_{M_{XVX}: \text{ (K x K)}} \text{ has rank K}
\]



Under the same assumptions as pooled OLS, the only difference in how we derive the estimator. To find the efficient estimator under these conditions, suppose that \(B'B = V^{-1}\), where \(B\) is some matrix. We can then define our model as:
\[
By_i = BX_i'\beta + Bv_{i}
\]
This model satisfies all of our assumptions: to see this, check Appendix (1) for a thorough handling.




Similar to pooled OLS, when applying the OLS estimator to our regressor we find it has the form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  & \hat{\beta}_{RE} = \left( X'V^{-1}X \right)^{-1}X'V^{-1}y  &&\text{RE estimator}\\
  & \hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta = \left( X'V^{-1}X \right)^{-1}X'V^{-1}v && \text{sampling error}
\end{aligned}
\]
To see the full derivation of the RE estimator and the sampling error, see Appendix (2)


To see that the RE estimator is an unbiased estimator, we want to show that \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{RE}] = \beta \Leftrightarrow \mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta] = 0\)
Thus, we simply need to take expectations of the sampling error:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta] &= \mathbb{E}\left[ X'V^{-1}X \right]^{-1}  \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}v] \\
&=  \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X \mid X]\right]^{-1}  \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}v \mid X]] && \text{via LIE}\\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[ X'V^{-1}X \right]^{-1}  \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}\mathbb{E}[v\mid X]] && \text{via LCE} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[v \mid X] = \mathbb{E}[f + u \mid X] && \text{via def} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[f \mid X] + \mathbb{E}[u \mid X] = 0 && \text{via assumption} \\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[ X'V^{-1}X \right]^{-1}  \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}\cdot 0] = 0 \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta &= \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \\
&= \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)}_{(1)}^{-1} \underbrace{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i}_{(2)} \\
(1):&  \text{ via the WLLN, this converges in probability:} \\
& \left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right) \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right] \\
& \text{via the CMT, this convergence implies that:} \\
& \left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right]^{-1} \\
(2):& \text{ via the WLLN, this converges in probability:} \\
& \left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \right) \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \right] \\
&\text{ which we know equals zero due to unbiasedness:} \\
& \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \right] = 0 \\
& \text{therefore, via Slutsky's Theorem,} \\
& \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right]^{-1} \cdot 0 = 0 \\
& \hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta \xrightarrow{p} 0 && \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



To derive the asymptotic normality of the RE estimator, we simply rescale the sampling error by \(\sqrt{N}\), s.t.:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{N}\left(\hat{\beta}_\text{RE} - \beta \right)& = \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i' V^{-1} X_i \right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i' V^{-1} v_i}_{(2)} \\
  & (1) \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[X' V^{-1} X]^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
  & (2) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(X' V^{-1}v) \right) \text{ via CLT} \\
  & \text{thus, via Slutsky's theorem, } \\
  \sqrt{N}\left(\hat{\beta}_\text{RE} - \beta \right)& \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}(X'V^{-1}vv'V^{-1}X)\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1} \right)
\end{aligned}
\]




Note that \(\mathbb{E}[vv' \mid X] = V\); thus, using the Linearity of Iterated Expectations, we can rewrite \(\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_{RE})\) as:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_\text{RE}) &= \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}\mathbb{E}[vv' \mid X]V^{-1}X]\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1} V V^{-1}X] \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X] \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, the RE estimator is the best linear and unbiased estimator (BLUE) under our given model and assumptions. For a formal proof, see Appendix (3)
Importantly: \(V^{-1}\) is unknown in reality; we need to compute an estimate of the matrix \(\hat{V}\) in order to construct \(\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_\text{RE})\). In other words, we need to find:
\[
\hat{V_i} = \mathbb{E}[ \hat{v}_i \hat{v}_i' \mid X ]
\]
In order to get an estimate of the variance, we thereby need to get estimates of the residuals from our model using an unbiased and consistent estimator. Fortunately, we already found that \(\hat{\beta}_{POLS}\) has these properties and thereby is a valid choice of an estimator! Hence, we can find \(v_iv_i' = (y_i - X_i' \beta)(y_i - X_i' \beta)'\).
However, we need to compute two separate estimates for the \(\hat{V}_i\) matrix:

\(\mathbb{E}[\widehat{v}_{it}^2 \mid X] = \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}\): diagonal elements (variance)
\(\mathbb{E}[\widehat{v_{it}v_{is}} \mid X] = \widehat{\sigma}_f^2, \forall_{ t \neq s}\): off-diagonal elements (co-variance)

To compute these estimates, we need to use our estimated residuals to construct the variance & co-variance elements composing each matrix, \(\forall_{i \in N}\):
\(\widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} = \frac{1}{NT-K} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{t=1}^T \widehat{v}_{it}^2\)
\(\widehat{\sigma}_f^2 = \frac{1}{\frac{NT(T-1)}{2}-K} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \sum_{s=t+1}^T \widehat{v_{it}v_{is}}\)






Note



Note the denominator term for our covariance terms; this simply comes from the fact that for each individual variance-covariance matrix, we are computing \(\frac{T^2 -T}{2}\) elements, since our matrix has dimensions \((T \times T)\). To compute the off-diagonal elements of a symmetric matrix, we need to calculate \(T^2\) elements, subtracted by the \(T\) diagonal elements, and then divide by 2 as we only need to estimate \(U \equiv L\). We then iterate through this process for all \(N\) individuals, and subtract by the number of \(K\) regressors in our model.


Note that the estimated \(\hat{V}_i\) variance-covariance matrix is for an individual \(i\) for all panels \(t= 1, 2, \dots , T\) and is thereby \((T \times T)\); the entire \(\hat{V}\) matrix consists of all \(\hat{V}_i\) matrices across all \(i= 1, 2, \dots, N\) individuals, giving it dimensions \((NT \times NT)\). It is given by the form:
\[
\underset{(NT \times NT)}{\hat{V}} =
\begin{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \cdots &  \widehat{\sigma_f^2} \\
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} & \cdots & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} \\
    \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \cdots & \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}
  \end{bmatrix}_{i=1} & 0 & \\
  0 & \begin{bmatrix}
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \cdots &  \widehat{\sigma_f^2} \\
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} & \cdots & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} \\
    \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \cdots & \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}
  \end{bmatrix}_{i=2} \\  &  & \ddots
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Thus, to find \(\hat{\sigma}_{\mu}\), we simply take the difference between the diagonal (variance) elements \(\widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}\) and the off-diagonal (covariance) elements \(\widehat{\sigma_f^2}\):
\[
\widehat{\sigma}_{\mu}^2 = \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} - \widehat{\sigma}_f^2
\]
In other words, we can simply retrieve the idiosyncratic variance terms by off-diagonal from the diagonal. Since the matrix is symmetric across all \(\hat{V}_i\) matrices, we simply only need to calculate \(\widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}\) and \(\widehat{\sigma_f^2}\) to fully determine the entire \((NT \times NT)\) matrix \(\hat{V}\). Furthermore, this equicorrelation structure implies that \(V^{-1}\) has a known closed-form, allowing us to replace full GLS inversion with the computationally equivalent quasi-demeaning transformation (see here: Appendix (4))
Finally, we plug in these \(\hat{V}\) estimates back into the RE estimator:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{RE} = \left(\sum X_i' \hat{V}{}^{-1} X_i \right)^{-1} \left(\sum X_i'\hat{V}{}^{-1} y_i  \right)
\]
We simply use the analogy principle to get the asymptotic variance matrix:
\[
\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_{RE}) =
\frac{1}{N} \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N  X_i' \hat{V}{}^{-1} X_i \right)^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[X_i' \hat{V}{}^{-1} X_i]^{-1}
= \text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_{RE})
\]






Note



Following Woolridge’s notation, this equivalently can be expressed as:
\(\hat{\beta}_{RE} \sim \mathcal{N}(\beta, \frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}[X_i' \hat{V}{}^{-1} X_i]^{-1} )\)





If we relax the assumption of homoskedasticity of the idiosyncratic error terms, we cannot reduce down the variance any further and thereby estimate the following “sandwich” form of the variance:
\[
\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_{RE}) =
\mathbb{E}\left[X_i'V^{-1}X_i\right]^{-1}\mathbb{E}\left[ X_i'V^{-1}v_iv_i'V^{-1}X_i\right] \mathbb{E}\left[ X_i'V^{-1}X_i\right]^{-1}
\]
To get estimates of the asymptotic variance, we follow a 2-stage process:

Apply Pooled OLS and collect \(\widehat{v_{it}}\), then use \(\widehat{v_{it}}\) to construct \(\widehat{\sigma_{f}^2}\) and \(\widehat{\sigma_{f}^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}\), giving us the invertible matrix \(\hat{V}\).
Apply RE estimator and collect \(\widehat{\widehat{v_{it}}}\); plug in \(\widehat{\widehat{v_{it}}}\) and \(\hat{V}{}^{-1}\) into the asymptotic variance formula \(\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_{RE})\).

More formally:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  & 1. \quad \widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_\text{POLS})^\text{CLUSTER(id)} =    \left(\sum X_i'X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum X_i'\hat{v}_i\hat{v}_i'X_i\right) \left(\sum X_i'X_i\right)^{-1} \\
  & 2. \quad  \widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_\text{RE})^\text{CLUSTER(id)} =    \left(\sum X_i'\hat{V}{}^{-1}X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum X_i'\hat{V}{}^{-1}\hat{\hat{v}}_i\hat{\hat{v}}_i'\hat{V}{}^{-1}X_i\right) \left(\sum X_i'\hat{V}{}^{-1}X_i\right)^{-1}
\end{aligned}
\]






Warning



Note the notation for our two stage-estimation process: CLUSTER(id)
This stands for ‘clustering on the individual level,’ allowing for arbitrary serial correlation within a given \(\begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{i}\), whilst maintaining independence across \(i = 1, 2, \dots, N\). In other words, we can treat a single individual’s timeline as a single “mega-observation,” allowing an individual \(i\) to be correlated with itself across periods in the panel.




What if we cluster on a higher level? Rather than the individual level, say we cluster on households, cities, countries, etc. Our asymptotic variance can simply be expressed as:
\[\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_{\text{RE}})^\text{CLUSTER(c)} =\left(\sum_c X_c'\hat{V}{}^{-1}X_c \right)^{-1} \left(\sum_c X_c'\hat{V}{}^{-1} \hat{\hat{v}}_c \hat{\hat{v}}_c' \hat{V}{}^{-1}X_c \right) \left(\sum_c X_c'\hat{V}{}^{-1}X_c \right)^{-1}\]
To better understand, imagine simply grouping together multiple different \(\begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{i}\) into a single ‘cluster’ based on some shared factor. For example, we would likely expect individuals within the same household to be correlated with one another; thus, we say that individuals \(\begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{1}\) and \(\begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{2}\) are both in \(c_1\), such that this matrix \(c_1\) “supersedes” the original \(\begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{1, } \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{2}\) matrices. This allows for arbitrary serial correlation between individuals in the cluster.
\[
V =
\begin{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{1} \\
  & \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{2} \end{bmatrix}_{c_1} & & \\
  & & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{3} \end{bmatrix}_{c_2} & & \\
  & & & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{4} \\
  & & & & \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{5} \end{bmatrix}_{c_3} \\
  & & & & & \ddots
\end{bmatrix}
\]






Warning



Note that we still need a sufficient number of clusters for asymptotic properties to hold. At least \(\geq\) 30, however, usually it is expected/found that ~50 is the standard. Any lower and we will need clustering bootstrap methods to construct robust standard errors.
Furthermore, we can do ‘multi-dimensional’ clustering; e.g., on industry, then households, etc. Of course we need even more data points for such a case.
Clustering is standard practice. Stata does it automatically for us.






In practice, nobody uses the random effects estimator; the assumption of random individual effects is too strong of an assumption. Typically, we expect for there to exist some correlation between the exogenous regressors and the unobserved effect(s). In other words, random effects treats the unobserved effect as a random variable.
This motivates the introduction of a new estimator, namely the Fixed Effects estimator that relaxes this assumption, by allowing for non-zero correlation between \(f_i\) and \(X_i\).

title: Random Effects
text: As we saw with the pooled OLS estimator, it yields a consistent and unbiased estimator but is not efficient, due to the serial correlation in the composite error induced by the unobserved effect. Thus, there exists an estimator that is efficient under similar conditions, known as the Random Effects estimator; this is the equivalent to the generalized least squares (GLS) estimator from finite sample OLS.

title: Random Effects
text:
Our assumptions here follow almost exactly the same from pooled OLS, with one slight change in assumption 5.


Same as before
\[
y_{it} = x_{it}'\beta + f_i + \mu_{it}
\]



Same as before
\[
\mathbb{E}[f_i \mid x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \cdots, x_{iT}] \equiv \mathbb{E}[f_i \mid X_i] = 0
\]



Same as before
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \cdots, x_{iT}, f_i] \equiv \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i] = 0
\]



Same as before
\[
\begin{cases}
  1. \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(f_i \mid X_i) = \sigma_{f}^2 &\text{Constant Variance in the Unobserved Error} \\
  2. \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i) = \sigma_{\mu}^2 & \text{Constant Variance in the Idiosyncratic Error} \\
  3. \mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\mu_{it}, \mu_{is}) = 0 \quad \forall_{t \neq s} & \text{No Serial Correlation}
\end{cases}
\]



SLIGHT MODIFICATION
\[
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i' V^{-1} X_i  \xrightarrow{p} \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(X_i'V^{-1}X_i)}_{M_{XVX}: \text{ (K x K)}} \text{ has rank K}
\]



Under the same assumptions as pooled OLS, the only difference in how we derive the estimator. To find the efficient estimator under these conditions, suppose that \(B'B = V^{-1}\), where \(B\) is some matrix. We can then define our model as:
\[
By_i = BX_i'\beta + Bv_{i}
\]
This model satisfies all of our assumptions: to see this, check Appendix (1) for a thorough handling.

title: Random Effects
text:
Similar to pooled OLS, when applying the OLS estimator to our regressor we find it has the form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  & \hat{\beta}_{RE} = \left( X'V^{-1}X \right)^{-1}X'V^{-1}y  &&\text{RE estimator}\\
  & \hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta = \left( X'V^{-1}X \right)^{-1}X'V^{-1}v && \text{sampling error}
\end{aligned}
\]
To see the full derivation of the RE estimator and the sampling error, see Appendix (2)


To see that the RE estimator is an unbiased estimator, we want to show that \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{RE}] = \beta \Leftrightarrow \mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta] = 0\)
Thus, we simply need to take expectations of the sampling error:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta] &= \mathbb{E}\left[ X'V^{-1}X \right]^{-1}  \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}v] \\
&=  \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X \mid X]\right]^{-1}  \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}v \mid X]] && \text{via LIE}\\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[ X'V^{-1}X \right]^{-1}  \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}\mathbb{E}[v\mid X]] && \text{via LCE} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[v \mid X] = \mathbb{E}[f + u \mid X] && \text{via def} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[f \mid X] + \mathbb{E}[u \mid X] = 0 && \text{via assumption} \\
&= \mathbb{E}\left[ X'V^{-1}X \right]^{-1}  \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}\cdot 0] = 0 \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta &= \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \\
&= \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)}_{(1)}^{-1} \underbrace{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i}_{(2)} \\
(1):&  \text{ via the WLLN, this converges in probability:} \\
& \left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right) \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right] \\
& \text{via the CMT, this convergence implies that:} \\
& \left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right]^{-1} \\
(2):& \text{ via the WLLN, this converges in probability:} \\
& \left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \right) \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \right] \\
&\text{ which we know equals zero due to unbiasedness:} \\
& \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \right] = 0 \\
& \text{therefore, via Slutsky's Theorem,} \\
& \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right]^{-1} \cdot 0 = 0 \\
& \hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta \xrightarrow{p} 0 && \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



To derive the asymptotic normality of the RE estimator, we simply rescale the sampling error by \(\sqrt{N}\), s.t.:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{N}\left(\hat{\beta}_\text{RE} - \beta \right)& = \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i' V^{-1} X_i \right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i' V^{-1} v_i}_{(2)} \\
  & (1) \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[X' V^{-1} X]^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
  & (2) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(X' V^{-1}v) \right) \text{ via CLT} \\
  & \text{thus, via Slutsky's theorem, } \\
  \sqrt{N}\left(\hat{\beta}_\text{RE} - \beta \right)& \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}(X'V^{-1}vv'V^{-1}X)\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1} \right)
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Random Effects
text:
Note that \(\mathbb{E}[vv' \mid X] = V\); thus, using the Linearity of Iterated Expectations, we can rewrite \(\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_{RE})\) as:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_\text{RE}) &= \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}\mathbb{E}[vv' \mid X]V^{-1}X]\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1} V V^{-1}X] \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X] \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X'V^{-1}X]^{-1}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, the RE estimator is the best linear and unbiased estimator (BLUE) under our given model and assumptions. For a formal proof, see Appendix (3)

\[
\hat{V_i} = \mathbb{E}[ \hat{v}_i \hat{v}_i' \mid X ]
\]
In order to get an estimate of the variance, we thereby need to get estimates of the residuals from our model using an unbiased and consistent estimator. Fortunately, we already found that \(\hat{\beta}_{POLS}\) has these properties and thereby is a valid choice of an estimator! Hence, we can find \(v_iv_i' = (y_i - X_i' \beta)(y_i - X_i' \beta)'\).

\(\mathbb{E}[\widehat{v}_{it}^2 \mid X] = \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}\): diagonal elements (variance)
\(\mathbb{E}[\widehat{v_{it}v_{is}} \mid X] = \widehat{\sigma}_f^2, \forall_{ t \neq s}\): off-diagonal elements (co-variance)

To compute these estimates, we need to use our estimated residuals to construct the variance & co-variance elements composing each matrix, \(\forall_{i \in N}\):
\(\widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} = \frac{1}{NT-K} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{t=1}^T \widehat{v}_{it}^2\)
\(\widehat{\sigma}_f^2 = \frac{1}{\frac{NT(T-1)}{2}-K} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \sum_{s=t+1}^T \widehat{v_{it}v_{is}}\)






Note



Note the denominator term for our covariance terms; this simply comes from the fact that for each individual variance-covariance matrix, we are computing \(\frac{T^2 -T}{2}\) elements, since our matrix has dimensions \((T \times T)\). To compute the off-diagonal elements of a symmetric matrix, we need to calculate \(T^2\) elements, subtracted by the \(T\) diagonal elements, and then divide by 2 as we only need to estimate \(U \equiv L\). We then iterate through this process for all \(N\) individuals, and subtract by the number of \(K\) regressors in our model.


Note that the estimated \(\hat{V}_i\) variance-covariance matrix is for an individual \(i\) for all panels \(t= 1, 2, \dots , T\) and is thereby \((T \times T)\); the entire \(\hat{V}\) matrix consists of all \(\hat{V}_i\) matrices across all \(i= 1, 2, \dots, N\) individuals, giving it dimensions \((NT \times NT)\). It is given by the form:
\[
\underset{(NT \times NT)}{\hat{V}} =
\begin{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \cdots &  \widehat{\sigma_f^2} \\
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} & \cdots & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} \\
    \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \cdots & \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}
  \end{bmatrix}_{i=1} & 0 & \\
  0 & \begin{bmatrix}
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \cdots &  \widehat{\sigma_f^2} \\
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} & \cdots & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} \\
    \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
    \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \widehat{\sigma_f^2} & \cdots & \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}
  \end{bmatrix}_{i=2} \\  &  & \ddots
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Thus, to find \(\hat{\sigma}_{\mu}\), we simply take the difference between the diagonal (variance) elements \(\widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}\) and the off-diagonal (covariance) elements \(\widehat{\sigma_f^2}\):
\[
\widehat{\sigma}_{\mu}^2 = \widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2} - \widehat{\sigma}_f^2
\]
In other words, we can simply retrieve the idiosyncratic variance terms by off-diagonal from the diagonal. Since the matrix is symmetric across all \(\hat{V}_i\) matrices, we simply only need to calculate \(\widehat{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}\) and \(\widehat{\sigma_f^2}\) to fully determine the entire \((NT \times NT)\) matrix \(\hat{V}\). Furthermore, this equicorrelation structure implies that \(V^{-1}\) has a known closed-form, allowing us to replace full GLS inversion with the computationally equivalent quasi-demeaning transformation (see here: Appendix (4))
Finally, we plug in these \(\hat{V}\) estimates back into the RE estimator:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{RE} = \left(\sum X_i' \hat{V}{}^{-1} X_i \right)^{-1} \left(\sum X_i'\hat{V}{}^{-1} y_i  \right)
\]
We simply use the analogy principle to get the asymptotic variance matrix:
\[
\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_{RE}) =
\frac{1}{N} \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N  X_i' \hat{V}{}^{-1} X_i \right)^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[X_i' \hat{V}{}^{-1} X_i]^{-1}
= \text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_{RE})
\]






Note



Following Woolridge’s notation, this equivalently can be expressed as:
\(\hat{\beta}_{RE} \sim \mathcal{N}(\beta, \frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}[X_i' \hat{V}{}^{-1} X_i]^{-1} )\)

title: Random Effects
text:
If we relax the assumption of homoskedasticity of the idiosyncratic error terms, we cannot reduce down the variance any further and thereby estimate the following “sandwich” form of the variance:
\[
\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_{RE}) =
\mathbb{E}\left[X_i'V^{-1}X_i\right]^{-1}\mathbb{E}\left[ X_i'V^{-1}v_iv_i'V^{-1}X_i\right] \mathbb{E}\left[ X_i'V^{-1}X_i\right]^{-1}
\]
To get estimates of the asymptotic variance, we follow a 2-stage process:

Apply Pooled OLS and collect \(\widehat{v_{it}}\), then use \(\widehat{v_{it}}\) to construct \(\widehat{\sigma_{f}^2}\) and \(\widehat{\sigma_{f}^2 + \sigma_{\mu}^2}\), giving us the invertible matrix \(\hat{V}\).
Apply RE estimator and collect \(\widehat{\widehat{v_{it}}}\); plug in \(\widehat{\widehat{v_{it}}}\) and \(\hat{V}{}^{-1}\) into the asymptotic variance formula \(\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_{RE})\).

More formally:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  & 1. \quad \widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_\text{POLS})^\text{CLUSTER(id)} =    \left(\sum X_i'X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum X_i'\hat{v}_i\hat{v}_i'X_i\right) \left(\sum X_i'X_i\right)^{-1} \\
  & 2. \quad  \widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_\text{RE})^\text{CLUSTER(id)} =    \left(\sum X_i'\hat{V}{}^{-1}X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum X_i'\hat{V}{}^{-1}\hat{\hat{v}}_i\hat{\hat{v}}_i'\hat{V}{}^{-1}X_i\right) \left(\sum X_i'\hat{V}{}^{-1}X_i\right)^{-1}
\end{aligned}
\]






Warning



Note the notation for our two stage-estimation process: CLUSTER(id)
This stands for ‘clustering on the individual level,’ allowing for arbitrary serial correlation within a given \(\begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{i}\), whilst maintaining independence across \(i = 1, 2, \dots, N\). In other words, we can treat a single individual’s timeline as a single “mega-observation,” allowing an individual \(i\) to be correlated with itself across periods in the panel.




What if we cluster on a higher level? Rather than the individual level, say we cluster on households, cities, countries, etc. Our asymptotic variance can simply be expressed as:
\[\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_{\text{RE}})^\text{CLUSTER(c)} =\left(\sum_c X_c'\hat{V}{}^{-1}X_c \right)^{-1} \left(\sum_c X_c'\hat{V}{}^{-1} \hat{\hat{v}}_c \hat{\hat{v}}_c' \hat{V}{}^{-1}X_c \right) \left(\sum_c X_c'\hat{V}{}^{-1}X_c \right)^{-1}\]
To better understand, imagine simply grouping together multiple different \(\begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{i}\) into a single ‘cluster’ based on some shared factor. For example, we would likely expect individuals within the same household to be correlated with one another; thus, we say that individuals \(\begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{1}\) and \(\begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{2}\) are both in \(c_1\), such that this matrix \(c_1\) “supersedes” the original \(\begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{1, } \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{2}\) matrices. This allows for arbitrary serial correlation between individuals in the cluster.
\[
V =
\begin{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{1} \\
  & \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{2} \end{bmatrix}_{c_1} & & \\
  & & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{3} \end{bmatrix}_{c_2} & & \\
  & & & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{4} \\
  & & & & \begin{bmatrix} V \end{bmatrix}_{5} \end{bmatrix}_{c_3} \\
  & & & & & \ddots
\end{bmatrix}
\]






Warning



Note that we still need a sufficient number of clusters for asymptotic properties to hold. At least \(\geq\) 30, however, usually it is expected/found that ~50 is the standard. Any lower and we will need clustering bootstrap methods to construct robust standard errors.
Furthermore, we can do ‘multi-dimensional’ clustering; e.g., on industry, then households, etc. Of course we need even more data points for such a case.
Clustering is standard practice. Stata does it automatically for us.

title: Random Effects
text:
In practice, nobody uses the random effects estimator; the assumption of random individual effects is too strong of an assumption. Typically, we expect for there to exist some correlation between the exogenous regressors and the unobserved effect(s). In other words, random effects treats the unobserved effect as a random variable.
This motivates the introduction of a new estimator, namely the Fixed Effects estimator that relaxes this assumption, by allowing for non-zero correlation between \(f_i\) and \(X_i\).

title: Random Effects
text:
1 RE Model Satisfies OLS Assumptions
To see that our transformed RE regression model satisfies our assumptions, let us check assumption-by-assumption. The check will only be for assumptions 2-5, as we explicitly defined the model to simply be a linear transformation of the original linear model (thus the linearity assumption is trivially satisfied).

1. Random Individual Effects
\[
\mathbb{E}[Bf_i \mid x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \cdots, x_{iT}] = B\mathbb{E}[f_i \mid X_i] = 0 \quad \text{via LCE}
\]
We know that \(B = V^{-\frac{1}{2}}\) and that \(V\) is a function of X, since \(V = \mathbb{E}[v_iv_i' | x_{it}]\) and we can rewrite \(v_i = y_i - X_i'\beta\). Thus, we can remove it from the expectation via the linearity of conditional expectations.


2. Strictly Exogenous Regressors
\[
\mathbb{E}[B\mu_{it} \mid x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \cdots, x_{iT}, f_i] = B\mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i] = 0 \quad \text{via LCE}
\]
Again, via the LCE we can remove the B matrix from the expectation and find that the assumption of strictly exogenous regressors holds.


3. Homoskedasticity
\[
\begin{aligned}
  & 1. \quad \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(Bf_i \mid X_i) =
  B \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(f_i \mid X_i) B' =
  V^{-1}\sigma_{f}^2 &\text{Constant Variance in the Unobserved Error} \\
  & 2. \quad \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i) = \sigma_{\mu}^2 & \text{Constant Variance in the Idiosyncratic Error} \\
  & 3.\quad \mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\mu_{it}, \mu_{is}) = 0 \quad \forall_{t \neq s} & \text{No Serial Correlation}
\end{aligned}
\]


4. Linearly Independent Regressors
We need to show that the rank condition holds for the transformed regressors \(X_i^* = BX_i\):
\[
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i^{*\prime} X_i^* = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N (BX_i)'(BX_i) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'B'BX_i = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i
\]
By the WLLN, this converges in probability:
\[
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[X_i'V^{-1}X_i] = M_{XVX}
\]
which has rank \(K\) by Assumption 5. \(\qquad \blacksquare\)

title: Random Effects
text:
2 Derivation of RE Estimator
Recall our transformed model: \(By_i = BX_i\beta + Bv_i\), where \(B'B = V^{-1}\). Since we showed in Appendix (1) that this model satisfies our OLS assumptions, we can apply OLS directly to the transformed data. Define \(y_i^* \equiv By_i\), \(X_i^* \equiv BX_i\), and \(v_i^* \equiv Bv_i\). The OLS estimator on the transformed model is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{RE} &= \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i^{*\prime} X_i^* \right)^{-1} \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i^{*\prime} y_i^* \right) \\
&= \left(\sum_{i=1}^N (BX_i)'(BX_i) \right)^{-1} \left(\sum_{i=1}^N (BX_i)'(By_i) \right) \\
&= \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'B'BX_i \right)^{-1} \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'B'By_i \right) \\
&= \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)^{-1} \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}y_i \right) \qquad \text{via } B'B = V^{-1}
\end{aligned}
\]
To derive the sampling error, substitute \(y_i = X_i\beta + v_i\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{RE} &= \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)^{-1} \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}(X_i\beta + v_i) \right) \\
&= \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)^{-1} \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i\beta + \sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \right) \\
&= \underbrace{\left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i\right)}_{= I_K}\beta + \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \\
&= \beta + \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{RE} - \beta = \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i \right)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}v_i \qquad \blacksquare
\]

title: Random Effects
section: 3 Proof of RE Estimator is BLUE
text:
3 Proof of RE Estimator is BLUE
We want to show that for any linear unbiased estimator \(\tilde{\beta}\), the difference \(\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\tilde{\beta}) - \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_{RE})\) is positive semi-definite.
Since we showed in Appendix (1) that the transformed model \(By_i = BX_i\beta + Bv_i\) satisfies the classical OLS assumptions, we can invoke the Gauss-Markov theorem on the transformed model directly.
By construction, \(B'B = V^{-1}\), so:
\[
\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(Bv_i \mid X_i) = B\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(v_i \mid X_i)B' = BVB'
\]
Since \(B = V^{-1/2}\), we have \(BVB' = V^{-1/2}VV^{-1/2} = I_T\). Thus the transformed errors are homoskedastic and serially uncorrelated.
Define \(y_i^* = By_i\), \(X_i^* = BX_i\), \(v_i^* = Bv_i\). Since \(\mathbb{E}[v_i^* \mid X_i^*] = 0\) and \(\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(v_i^* \mid X_i^*) = I_T\), the Gauss-Markov theorem tells us that OLS on the transformed data is BLUE:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{OLS}^* = \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i^{*\prime}X_i^*\right)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i^{*\prime}y_i^*
\]
has the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators in the transformed model.
As shown in Appendix (2):
\[
\hat{\beta}_{OLS}^* = \left(\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}X_i\right)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i'V^{-1}y_i = \hat{\beta}_{RE}
\]
Let \(\tilde{\beta} = \sum_{i=1}^N A_i y_i\) be any linear unbiased estimator. Since \(B\) is invertible, we can write \(y_i = B^{-1}y_i^*\), so:
\[
\tilde{\beta} = \sum_{i=1}^N A_i B^{-1} y_i^* = \sum_{i=1}^N \tilde{A}_i y_i^*
\]
where \(\tilde{A}_i \equiv A_iB^{-1}\). This is a linear estimator in the transformed model. If \(\tilde{\beta}\) is unbiased for \(\beta\) in the original model, it is also unbiased in the transformed model.
By Gauss-Markov, no linear unbiased estimator in the transformed model can have a smaller variance than \(\hat{\beta}_{OLS}^*\). Since every linear unbiased estimator in the original model corresponds to one in the transformed model (Step 4), and \(\hat{\beta}_{OLS}^* = \hat{\beta}_{RE}\) (Step 3):
\[
\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\tilde{\beta} \mid X) - \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\hat{\beta}_{RE} \mid X) \geq 0 \quad \text{(positive semi-definite)}
\]
for all linear unbiased \(\tilde{\beta}\). Therefore \(\hat{\beta}_{RE}\) is BLUE. \(\qquad \blacksquare\)

title: Random Effects
text:
4 Quasi-Demeaning Equivalence
We show that the RE-GLS estimator \(\hat{\beta}_{GLS} = \left(\sum_i X_i' V_i^{-1} X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_i X_i' V_i^{-1} y_i\right)\) is algebraically equivalent to pooled OLS on quasi-demeaned data \(\tilde{z}_{it} = z_{it} - \hat{\theta} \bar{z}_i\).
Define the two \((T \times T)\) projection matrices:

\(P\): the between (averaging) matrix, which maps \(z_i\) to its time-mean \(\bar{z}_i\), repeated \(T\) times.
\(M \equiv I_T - P\): the within (annihilator) matrix, which maps \(z_i\) to its deviations from the time-mean \((z_{it} - \bar{z}_i)\).

These are orthogonal idempotent: \(M^2 = M\), \(P^2 = P\), \(MP = 0\), and \(M + P = I_T\).
Under our assumptions, \(V_i = \sigma_\mu^2 I_T + T\sigma_f^2 P\). Substituting \(I_T = M + P\):
\[
V_i = \sigma_\mu^2(M + P) + T\sigma_f^2 P = \sigma_\mu^2 M + (\sigma_\mu^2 + T\sigma_f^2)P
\]
Since \(M\) and \(P\) are orthogonal projectors that span \(I_T\), the inverse is:
\[
V_i^{-1} = \frac{1}{\sigma_\mu^2}M + \frac{1}{\sigma_\mu^2 + T\sigma_f^2}P
\]
To verify: \(V_i V_i^{-1} = \left[\sigma_\mu^2 M + (\sigma_\mu^2 + T\sigma_f^2)P\right]\left[\frac{1}{\sigma_\mu^2}M + \frac{1}{\sigma_\mu^2 + T\sigma_f^2}P\right] = MM + PP = M + P = I_T\), where cross-terms vanish by \(MP = 0\).
For any vector \(z_i = (z_{i1}, \dots, z_{iT})'\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
V_i^{-1}z_i &= \frac{1}{\sigma_\mu^2}Mz_i + \frac{1}{\sigma_\mu^2 + T\sigma_f^2}Pz_i \\
&= \frac{1}{\sigma_\mu^2}\left[Mz_i + \frac{\sigma_\mu^2}{\sigma_\mu^2 + T\sigma_f^2}Pz_i\right] \\
&= \frac{1}{\sigma_\mu^2}\left[(z_{it} - \bar{z}_i) + \frac{\sigma_\mu^2}{\sigma_\mu^2 + T\sigma_f^2}\bar{z}_i\right] \\
&= \frac{1}{\sigma_\mu^2}\left[z_{it} - \left(1 - \frac{\sigma_\mu^2}{\sigma_\mu^2 + T\sigma_f^2}\right)\bar{z}_i\right]
\end{aligned}
\]
Let:
\[
\theta \equiv 1 - \frac{\sigma_\mu^2}{\sigma_\mu^2 + T\sigma_f^2} = \frac{T\sigma_f^2}{\sigma_\mu^2 + T\sigma_f^2} \in [0, 1]
\]
Then Step 3 gives \(V_i^{-1}z_i = \frac{1}{\sigma_\mu^2}(z_{it} - \theta\bar{z}_i) \equiv \frac{1}{\sigma_\mu^2}\tilde{z}_{it}\), where \(\tilde{z}_{it}\) is the quasi-demeaned observation.
Note the boundary behavior: as \(\sigma_f^2 \to \infty\), \(\theta \to 1\) and RE collapses to the FE within estimator; as \(\sigma_f^2 \to 0\), \(\theta \to 0\) and RE collapses to pooled OLS.
Applying Step 4 to both \(X_i\) and \(y_i\):
\[
X_i'V_i^{-1}y_i = \frac{1}{\sigma_\mu^2}\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{y}_i, \qquad X_i'V_i^{-1}X_i = \frac{1}{\sigma_\mu^2}\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i
\]
Substituting into the GLS formula:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{GLS} &= \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{1}{\sigma_\mu^2}\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{1}{\sigma_\mu^2}\tilde{X}_i'\tilde{y}_i\right) \\
&= \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{X}_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^N \tilde{X}_i'\tilde{y}_i\right) \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]
The \(\frac{1}{\sigma_\mu^2}\) scalar appears in both terms and cancels, so the RE estimator reduces to pooled OLS on the quasi-demeaned data.

title: First Differences
text:
The FE estimator eliminates \(f_i\) by subtracting individual-specific time means. First differencing is an alternative: subtract consecutive observations rather than group means. Both transformations remove \(f_i\) and yield consistent estimators under the same exogeneity assumption, but they impose different homoskedasticity conditions and differ in efficiency depending on the structure of \(\mu_{it}\).
Under the FE homoskedasticity assumption (\(\mu_{it}\) i.i.d. over \(t\)), first differencing introduces MA(1) serial correlation into \(\Delta\mu_{it}\) and FE is more efficient. Under the FD homoskedasticity assumption (\(\Delta\mu_{it}\) i.i.d., i.e., \(\mu_{it}\) follows a random walk), FD is the more efficient estimator. When \(T = 2\), the two estimators are numerically identical.





Same as before:
\[
y_{it} = \mathbf{x}_{it}'\beta + \mathbf{z}_{i}'\gamma + f_i + \mu_{it}
\]



Same as FE:
\[
E(f_i \mid X_i) \neq 0
\]
\(f_i\) can be correlated with the regressors and is eliminated by first differencing.



Same as before:
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid \mathbf{x}_{i1}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{iT}, f_i] \equiv \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i] = 0
\]



NEW. The homoskedasticity condition is imposed on the first-differenced error \(\Delta\mu_{it} = \mu_{it} - \mu_{i,t-1}\):
\[
\begin{cases}
1. \ \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\Delta\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i) = \sigma_{e}^2 & \text{Constant Variance After Differencing} \\
2. \ \mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\Delta\mu_{it}, \Delta\mu_{is} \mid X_i, f_i) = 0 \quad \forall_{t \neq s} & \text{No Serial Correlation After Differencing}
\end{cases}
\]
\(\star\) This implies \(\mu_{it} = \mu_{i,t-1} + e_{it}\) where \(e_{it}\) is i.i.d. with variance \(\sigma_e^2\); in other words, \(\mu_{it}\) follows a random walk. This is qualitatively different from the FE homoskedasticity assumption and is not nested in it (for \(T > 2\)).



NEW. The rank condition is imposed on the first-differenced regressors \(\Delta X_i\):
\[
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i \xrightarrow{p} \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(\Delta X_i'\Delta X_i)}_{M_{\Delta X \Delta X}: \text{ (K x K)}} \text{ has rank } K^*
\]
Where \(K^*\) represents the number of time-varying regressors. Time-constant regressors satisfy \(\Delta z_i = 0\) and cannot enter the first-differenced model; like FE, FD cannot identify the coefficients on time-invariant covariates.



Taking first differences of the model for \(t = 2, \ldots, T\):
\[
\underbrace{y_{it} - y_{i,t-1}}_{\Delta y_{it}} = \underbrace{(\mathbf{x}_{it} - \mathbf{x}_{i,t-1})'}_{\Delta\mathbf{x}_{it}'}\beta + \underbrace{(\mathbf{z}_{i} - \mathbf{z}_{i})}_{=0}'\gamma + \underbrace{(f_i - f_i)}_{=0} +  \underbrace{(\mu_{it} - \mu_{i,t-1})}_{\Delta\mu_{it}}
\]
since \(\Delta f_i = f_i - f_i = 0\) and \(\Delta \mathbf{z}_{i} = \mathbf{z}_{i} - \mathbf{z}_{i} =0\). In matrix notation, the \((T-1) \times T\) first-difference matrix is:
\[
D_T = \begin{bmatrix}
-1 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & -1 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & \cdots & 0 & -1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
so that \(\Delta\mathbf{y}_i = D_T\mathbf{y}_i\), \(\Delta X_i = D_T X_i\), and \(\Delta\mu_i = D_T\mu_i\). We lose one time period per individual, giving \(N(T-1)\) total observations.
The FD estimator is OLS applied to the first-differenced model:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{FD} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta X_i'\Delta\mathbf{y}_i\right)
\]






The sampling error is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta &= \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta\mathbf{y}_i - \beta \\
&= \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\sum_i \Delta X_i'(\Delta X_i\beta + \Delta\mu_i) - \beta \\
&= \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking conditional expectations:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta \mid X, f] &= \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\sum_i \Delta X_i' \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mu_i \mid X_i, f_i]}_{\text{=0 via A3}} = 0 \\
\Rightarrow \mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{FD}] &= \beta \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i}_{(2)} \\
(1) &\xrightarrow{p} M_{\Delta X \Delta X}^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
(2) &\xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[\Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i] = 0 \text{ via LLN and strict exogeneity (A3)} \\
\hat{\beta}_{FD} &\xrightarrow{p} \beta \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta) &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i}_{(2)} \\
(1) &\xrightarrow{p} M_{\Delta X \Delta X}^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
(2) &\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i)\right) \text{ via CLT}
\end{aligned}
\]
Under assumption 4, \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mu_i\Delta\mu_i' \mid X_i, f_i] = \sigma_e^2 I_{T-1}\), so \(\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i) = \sigma_e^2 M_{\Delta X \Delta X}\). Thus:
\[
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \sigma_e^2 M_{\Delta X \Delta X}^{-1}\right) \qquad \blacksquare
\]


The A\(\mathbb{V}\)AR under assumption 4 is \(\sigma_e^2 M_{\Delta X \Delta X}^{-1}\). To estimate \(\sigma_e^2\), compute FD residuals \(\hat{e}_{it} = \Delta y_{it} - \Delta\mathbf{x}_{it}'\hat{\beta}_{FD}\) and use:
\[
\hat{\sigma}_e^2 = \frac{1}{N(T-1) - K}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=2}^T \hat{e}_{it}^2
\]
Using the analogy principle:
\[
\hat{\sigma}_e^2\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} \sigma_e^2\,\mathbb{E}[\Delta X_i'\Delta X_i]^{-1}
\]
If assumption 4 fails, we instead use the cluster-robust ‘sandwich’ estimator:
\[
\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_{FD}) = \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\hat{e}_i\hat{e}_i'\Delta X_i\right)\left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}
\]
\(\star\) In practice, standard errors should always be clustered at the individual level in a first-difference model, since the true structure of \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mu_i\Delta\mu_i']\) is generally unknown.






When \(T = 2\): FE and FD produce numerically identical estimates and inference. (to see this, check out Q3 of PS1)
When \(T > 2\) and \(\mu_{it}\) is i.i.d. over \(t\): FE is more efficient. Differencing introduces MA(1) serial correlation into \(\Delta\mu_{it}\), which loses information relative to the within transformation.
When \(T > 2\) and \(\mu_{it}\) follows a random walk: FD is more efficient, since \(\Delta\mu_{it} = e_{it}\) is then i.i.d. and assumption 4 holds exactly.
If FE and FD estimates differ in ways that cannot be attributed to sampling error, this signals a violation of strict exogeneity: if \(\mu_{it}\) is correlated with \(\mathbf{x}_{is}\) for any \(t\) and \(s\), both estimators are inconsistent but will generally have different probability limits.

To see the difference in FE and FD being blue under different assumptions of serial correlation of the error terms, suppose that \(\mu_{it}\)is serially uncorrelated such that \(\text{cov}(\mu_{it}, \mu_{is}) = 0, \quad \forall_{t \neq s}\).
In this case, estimating the variance-covariance matrix on the first-differenced idiosyncratic errors takes the following form:
\[
\mathbb{E}[\Delta \mu_i ' \Delta \mu_i \mid X_i] = \sigma_{\mu}^2
\begin{bmatrix}
  2 & -1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
  -1 & 2 & -1 & \cdots & 0 \\
  0 & -1 & 2 & \ddots & \vdots \\
  \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & -1 \\
  0 & 0 & \cdots & -1 & 2
\end{bmatrix}
\]
To derive this matrix, we simply calculate the variance-covariance between first-differenced errors at different \(t\):
\[
\begin{align}
\text{1. Diagonal } (t=2):
  & \quad \mathbb{E}[\Delta \mu_{i2} \Delta \mu_{i2} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[(\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i1}) (\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i1}) \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i2}\mu_{i2} - 2\mu_{i2}\mu_{i1} + \mu_{i1}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i2}^2 \mid X_i]  - 2\mathbb{E}[\mu_{i2}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] + \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i1}^2 \mid X_i] \\
  &= \sigma_{\mu}^2 - 0 + \sigma_{\mu}^2 = 2\sigma_{\mu}^2
  \\ \\
  \text{2. Off-Diagonal }(t=3):
  & \quad \mathbb{E}[\Delta \mu_{i3} \Delta \mu_{i2} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[(\mu_{i3} - \mu_{i2}) (\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i1}) \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i3}\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i3}\mu_{i1} - \mu_{i2}\mu_{i2} +  \mu_{i2}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i3}\mu_{i2} \mid X_i]  - \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i3}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] - \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i2}^2 \mid X_i] + \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i2}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] \\
  &= 0 - 0 - \sigma_{\mu}^2 + 0 = -\sigma_{\mu}^2
  \\ \\
  \text{3. Off-Diagonal }(t \geq 4):
  & \quad \mathbb{E}[\Delta \mu_{i4} \Delta \mu_{i2} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[(\mu_{i4} - \mu_{i3}) (\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i1}) \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i4}\mu_{i2} - \mu_{i4}\mu_{i1} - \mu_{i3}\mu_{i2} +  \mu_{i3}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i4}\mu_{i2} \mid X_i]  - \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i4}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] - \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i3}\mu_{i2} \mid X_i] + \mathbb{E}[\mu_{i3}\mu_{i1} \mid X_i] \\
  &= 0 - 0 - 0 + 0 = 0
\end{align}
\]
Thus, if \(\mu_{it}\) are i.i.d. (no serial correlation) rather than a random walk, applying FD now introduces serial correlation! Hence, FE would be BLUE.


There exists a third case wherein the idiosyncratic errors are serially correlated, but do NOT follow a random walk.






Warning



In reality, it is very hard for the random walk assumption to hold in this setting; it would imply that a shock from 10-20 years ago is still perfectly persistent today, with no decay whatsoever.


More formally, \(\mu_{it} = \rho \mu_{it-1} + e_{it}\) where \(0 < \rho < 1\); this means our errors follow an AR(1) error structure (see ARMA notes for an extensive overview of AR(p) and MA(q) models). \(\rho\) is a measure of “persistence,” telling us how much a shock from last period (\(t-1\)) is carried over to today, \(t\). When \(\rho\) is between zero and one, the shock decays over time, eventually converging to zero, determined by how close the value is to zero.
In such a case, neither FD nor FE are BLUE! As a result, if we run either estimator without corrections, our standard errors will be incorrectly estimated (typically underestimated). This leads to inflated t-statistics, artificially tight confidence intervals, and a high risk of Type I errors (finding statistical significance where there is none).
While neither estimator is BLUE, their relative efficiency depends entirely on the value of \(\rho\):

As \(\rho \rightarrow 0\), FE becomes closer to being efficient.
As \(\rho \rightarrow 1\), FD becomes closer to being efficient.
If \(\rho \approx 0.5\), both estimators suffer from significant inefficiency.

There are two different approaches to take when dealing with such a situation:





In modern empirical practice, researchers generally care more about consistency than absolute efficiency, provided they can get inference right.
The idea here is to stick with the Fixed Effects (FE) estimator (or FD, if \(\rho\) is empirically very high), but now estimate the model using clustered (robust) standard errors.
Clustering here allows the variance-covariance matrix to be completely agnostic about the exact nature of the serial correlation within an pre-defined cluster. It corrects the standard errors for any pattern of autocorrelation (and heteroskedasticity) over time.



To strictly achieve BLUE (or asymptotically efficient estimates), you must explicitly model the AR(1) process using Feasible Generalized Least Squares (FGLS). The process is multi-step:

Estimate the model using FE to get consistent residuals.
Use those residuals to get \(\hat{\rho}\).
Apply a quasi-differencing transforatmion to the panel data. Instead of subtracting 100% of the previous period (like FD) or the total average (like FE), you subtract \(\hat{\rho}\) of the previous period:

\[
y_{it}− \hat{\rho} y_{it-1} = (x_{it}−\hat{\rho}x_{it−1})'\beta + f_i(1−\hat{\rho})+e_{it}
\]
Note: FGLS requires strict assumptions about the exact structure of the error variance. If your estimate of \(\rho\) is wrong, or if the true process is actually AR(2) or MA(1), FGLS can perform worse than FE.

title: First Differences
text:
The FE estimator eliminates \(f_i\) by subtracting individual-specific time means. First differencing is an alternative: subtract consecutive observations rather than group means. Both transformations remove \(f_i\) and yield consistent estimators under the same exogeneity assumption, but they impose different homoskedasticity conditions and differ in efficiency depending on the structure of \(\mu_{it}\).
Under the FE homoskedasticity assumption (\(\mu_{it}\) i.i.d. over \(t\)), first differencing introduces MA(1) serial correlation into \(\Delta\mu_{it}\) and FE is more efficient. Under the FD homoskedasticity assumption (\(\Delta\mu_{it}\) i.i.d., i.e., \(\mu_{it}\) follows a random walk), FD is the more efficient estimator. When \(T = 2\), the two estimators are numerically identical.

title: First Differences
text:
Same as before:
\[
y_{it} = \mathbf{x}_{it}'\beta + \mathbf{z}_{i}'\gamma + f_i + \mu_{it}
\]



Same as FE:
\[
E(f_i \mid X_i) \neq 0
\]
\(f_i\) can be correlated with the regressors and is eliminated by first differencing.



Same as before:
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid \mathbf{x}_{i1}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{iT}, f_i] \equiv \mathbb{E}[\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i] = 0
\]



NEW. The homoskedasticity condition is imposed on the first-differenced error \(\Delta\mu_{it} = \mu_{it} - \mu_{i,t-1}\):
\[
\begin{cases}
1. \ \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\Delta\mu_{it} \mid X_i, f_i) = \sigma_{e}^2 & \text{Constant Variance After Differencing} \\
2. \ \mathbb{C}\text{ov}(\Delta\mu_{it}, \Delta\mu_{is} \mid X_i, f_i) = 0 \quad \forall_{t \neq s} & \text{No Serial Correlation After Differencing}
\end{cases}
\]
\(\star\) This implies \(\mu_{it} = \mu_{i,t-1} + e_{it}\) where \(e_{it}\) is i.i.d. with variance \(\sigma_e^2\); in other words, \(\mu_{it}\) follows a random walk. This is qualitatively different from the FE homoskedasticity assumption and is not nested in it (for \(T > 2\)).



NEW. The rank condition is imposed on the first-differenced regressors \(\Delta X_i\):
\[
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i \xrightarrow{p} \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(\Delta X_i'\Delta X_i)}_{M_{\Delta X \Delta X}: \text{ (K x K)}} \text{ has rank } K^*
\]
Where \(K^*\) represents the number of time-varying regressors. Time-constant regressors satisfy \(\Delta z_i = 0\) and cannot enter the first-differenced model; like FE, FD cannot identify the coefficients on time-invariant covariates.



Taking first differences of the model for \(t = 2, \ldots, T\):
\[
\underbrace{y_{it} - y_{i,t-1}}_{\Delta y_{it}} = \underbrace{(\mathbf{x}_{it} - \mathbf{x}_{i,t-1})'}_{\Delta\mathbf{x}_{it}'}\beta + \underbrace{(\mathbf{z}_{i} - \mathbf{z}_{i})}_{=0}'\gamma + \underbrace{(f_i - f_i)}_{=0} +  \underbrace{(\mu_{it} - \mu_{i,t-1})}_{\Delta\mu_{it}}
\]
since \(\Delta f_i = f_i - f_i = 0\) and \(\Delta \mathbf{z}_{i} = \mathbf{z}_{i} - \mathbf{z}_{i} =0\). In matrix notation, the \((T-1) \times T\) first-difference matrix is:
\[
D_T = \begin{bmatrix}
-1 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & -1 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & \cdots & 0 & -1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
so that \(\Delta\mathbf{y}_i = D_T\mathbf{y}_i\), \(\Delta X_i = D_T X_i\), and \(\Delta\mu_i = D_T\mu_i\). We lose one time period per individual, giving \(N(T-1)\) total observations.
The FD estimator is OLS applied to the first-differenced model:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{FD} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta X_i'\Delta\mathbf{y}_i\right)
\]

title: First Differences
text:
The sampling error is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta &= \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta\mathbf{y}_i - \beta \\
&= \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\sum_i \Delta X_i'(\Delta X_i\beta + \Delta\mu_i) - \beta \\
&= \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking conditional expectations:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta \mid X, f] &= \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\sum_i \Delta X_i' \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mu_i \mid X_i, f_i]}_{\text{=0 via A3}} = 0 \\
\Rightarrow \mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{FD}] &= \beta \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i}_{(2)} \\
(1) &\xrightarrow{p} M_{\Delta X \Delta X}^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
(2) &\xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[\Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i] = 0 \text{ via LLN and strict exogeneity (A3)} \\
\hat{\beta}_{FD} &\xrightarrow{p} \beta \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta) &= \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}}_{(1)} \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i}_{(2)} \\
(1) &\xrightarrow{p} M_{\Delta X \Delta X}^{-1} \text{ via LLN and CMT} \\
(2) &\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i)\right) \text{ via CLT}
\end{aligned}
\]
Under assumption 4, \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mu_i\Delta\mu_i' \mid X_i, f_i] = \sigma_e^2 I_{T-1}\), so \(\mathbb{V}\text{ar}(\Delta X_i'\Delta\mu_i) = \sigma_e^2 M_{\Delta X \Delta X}\). Thus:
\[
\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta}_{FD} - \beta) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \sigma_e^2 M_{\Delta X \Delta X}^{-1}\right) \qquad \blacksquare
\]


The A\(\mathbb{V}\)AR under assumption 4 is \(\sigma_e^2 M_{\Delta X \Delta X}^{-1}\). To estimate \(\sigma_e^2\), compute FD residuals \(\hat{e}_{it} = \Delta y_{it} - \Delta\mathbf{x}_{it}'\hat{\beta}_{FD}\) and use:
\[
\hat{\sigma}_e^2 = \frac{1}{N(T-1) - K}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=2}^T \hat{e}_{it}^2
\]
Using the analogy principle:
\[
\hat{\sigma}_e^2\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1} \xrightarrow{p} \sigma_e^2\,\mathbb{E}[\Delta X_i'\Delta X_i]^{-1}
\]
If assumption 4 fails, we instead use the cluster-robust ‘sandwich’ estimator:
\[
\widehat{\text{A}\mathbb{V}\text{ar}}(\hat{\beta}_{FD}) = \left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\hat{e}_i\hat{e}_i'\Delta X_i\right)\left(\sum_i \Delta X_i'\Delta X_i\right)^{-1}
\]
\(\star\) In practice, standard errors should always be clustered at the individual level in a first-difference model, since the true structure of \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mu_i\Delta\mu_i']\) is generally unknown.

text:

Estimate the model using FE to get consistent residuals.
Use those residuals to get \(\hat{\rho}\).
Apply a quasi-differencing transforatmion to the panel data. Instead of subtracting 100% of the previous period (like FD) or the total average (like FE), you subtract \(\hat{\rho}\) of the previous period:

\[

\]
